column4: The section's vertical axis says ascent comes by turning toward the earthbound; 7:176 says the man could have been raised by the signs but instead “أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ”. This names the same reversal from elevation to attachment to earth.

The section describes the Qur'anic choice between ascent and remaining pressed down; 9:38 rebukes those summoned to go forth who “اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ”, making attachment to earth a chosen failure to move.

The section sets the low, earth-pressed words against the surah's raised path; 67:22 contrasts one who walks “مُكِبًّا عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ” with one walking upright on a straight path, giving bodily form to the same low/upright divide.

The section's lexicon identifies لبد (ل ب د, B001–B002) as things piled and pressed together; 72:19 uses “لِبَدًا” for the crowd almost piling onto God's servant as he rises to call on Him. It is the Qur'an's direct occurrence of the section's crowded heap-word.

The section's dictionary gloss for miskīn (س ك ن, B001) links the word to lost movement; 2:273 describes needy people who “لَا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ ضَرْبًا فِي الْأَرْضِ”. Their inability to travel makes the earth-bound poverty image concrete.

The section connects piled wealth, dust, rain-compacted ground, and giving to the poor. In 2:264, dust on a smooth rock is swept bare by a downpour after showy charity, so an apparent covering and expenditure leave no rooted result.

The section says the poor man's soil is also the rich man's measure of wealth and recalls the wish to become dust; 78:40 gives the denier's “يَا لَيْتَنِي كُنْتُ تُرَابًا” after seeing what his hands sent ahead, reversing poverty's dust into a wished-for refuge.

The section's lexicon says turbah for the dead is a grave (ت ر ب, B001) and traces البلد to grave or soil (ب ل د, B001); 20:55 says humanity is created from earth, returned to it, and brought out from it, placing both wealth and poverty under the same mortal ground.
The section puts wealth and the soil-bound poor on one horizontal plane; 28:81 makes Qarun's great wealth end when he and his house are swallowed by the earth, a stark reversal of riches as security.
The section's image culminates in feeding the miskīn; the garden owners in 68:24 plan “أَنْ لَا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا الْيَوْمَ ... مِسْكِينٌ”, turning abundant produce into a boundary against the poor.

The section pairs one stuck to earth through abundance with one through want; after the garden owners exclude the poor, 68:27 has them recognize “بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ”, reversing their former position into deprivation.
The section places abundant wealth and the needy on the same ground; 89:15 shows a person mistaking expanded provision for honor, exposing wealth as a measure that can mislead rather than lift him.

Where the section's poor person is pressed down by lack, 89:16 shows a person mistaking restricted provision for humiliation. The next verses correct both readings by turning to treatment of the orphan and poor.
The section says ascent is made by bending toward those pressed down; 89:17 rebukes people who “لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ”, naming the failure to honor a vulnerable person.
The section's steep-pass deeds include feeding the poor; 89:18 says people do not urge one another to feed “الْمِسْكِينِ”, the direct ethical opposite of bending toward the earthbound needy.

The section sets charity beside a man's claim about consuming heaps of wealth; 89:19 condemns consuming inheritance greedily (“أَكْلًا لَمًّا”), showing accumulated property turned inward instead of toward the needy.

The section's lexicon explains لبد (ل ب د, B002) with the dictionary form جمًّا, abundant; 89:20 uses “حُبًّا جَمًّا” for overwhelming love of wealth, directly clarifying the section's “wealth piled in abundance” image.
The section's piled مال and its grave/soil senses meet in 102:1–2: “التَّكَاثُرُ” is competition in increase, and this ayah makes that accumulation the distraction that precedes the grave.
The section traces البلد and turbah to burial ground; 102:2 says people continue competing “حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ”. The grave ends the earthly contest over abundance.
The section's “مَالًا لُّبَدًا” is wealth massed together; 104:2 depicts a person who gathers wealth and counts it (“جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ”), a close image of amassed property.

The section sets material abundance beside the dust-bound poor; 104:3 exposes the gathered man's false security, “يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ”, while the section's earthy and grave senses place wealth under mortality.

The section names freeing a captive and feeding an orphan or miskīn as the deeds that cross the steep pass; 2:177 directly joins giving wealth to kin, orphans, needy people, travelers, and freeing people from bondage.

The section opposes piled wealth to need and points toward feeding; 6:141 ties the earth's harvest to giving its due on harvest day and forbids waste, turning produce from private abundance toward a claim beyond the owner.
The section's upward passage is concrete help for the poor; 17:26 commands giving the miskīn and traveler their due, making the earthbound person a rightful recipient of wealth.

The section's BLD entry describes a camel putting its chest on the ground when it kneels; 22:36 pictures sacrificial camels whose sides fall, then commands people to eat and feed the needy. The animal's lowering becomes provision for others.

The section pairs material abundance with a person stuck in dust; 51:19 says the believers' wealth contains a known right for “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ”, giving the deprived a claim within the rich person's property.
The section presents abundance and poverty together and makes aid the ascent; 70:24 says the faithful have a known share in their wealth, which 70:25 identifies for the asker and deprived.
The section's toprağa yapışmış miskīn is one of the people toward whom the steep pass bends; 70:25 names the share in the preceding ayah as belonging to “السَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ”.

The section's steep-pass sequence frees a captive and feeds the needy; 76:8 depicts people giving food “مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا”, bringing the miskīn, orphan, and captive together as recipients.

The section pairs wealth pressed to earth with a poor person pressed into soil; 93:8 recalls that God found the Prophet in need and made him self-sufficient, connecting provision to the following commands about vulnerable people.
The section says elevation requires turning toward the lowly; 93:9 commands, “فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ”, giving a concrete response to vulnerability.
The section's poor person is a figure to whom one must bend; 93:10 says not to repel the asker (“السَّائِلَ”), making the response to need explicit.
The section locates the steep pass in caring for the vulnerable; 107:2 describes the denier as one who thrusts the orphan away, a direct reversal of that care.
The section names feeding the miskīn as a way upward; 107:3 condemns failing even to urge “طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ”, the precise opposite of that act.
The section's deeds include feeding the poor in a day of hunger; 74:44 gives the condemned speakers' own explanation: “وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ”.

The section makes care of the miskīn part of the difficult ascent; 69:34 describes the condemned person as one who did not urge feeding “الْمِسْكِينِ”, a direct counterpart to the section's ethical turn.

The section turns wealth from a boast into help for the earthbound poor; in 36:47, disbelievers refuse to feed those in need by asking whether they should feed people God could feed, a pointed reversal of wealth as a means of mercy.

The section sets the wealthy and needy side by side on the same plane; 59:7 explains distribution of communal wealth so it will not remain “دُولَةً بَيْنَ الْأَغْنِيَاءِ”, supplying a concrete boundary against wealth piling among the rich.
The section's ascent comes through giving to the needy; 2:271 praises giving to the poor, including when concealed, contrasting aid with a public display of spending.

Where 2:264's showy charity leaves dust-covered rock bare, 2:265 compares sincere spending to a garden on high ground (“بِرَبْوَةٍ”) that yields fruit in heavy rain or drizzle. It links giving with elevation and lasting yield.
The section distinguishes piled wealth from the deeds that raise a person; 18:46 calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life but says enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope.

The section's wealth and soil image concerns what is pressed down and what can rise; 57:20 joins boasting and competition in wealth to vegetation that flourishes after rain, yellows, and becomes debris, setting passing abundance against what endures.
The section's wealth-mass image is sharpened by Qarun: 28:76 depicts the immense weight of his treasure keys, making abundance itself a burden before the earth swallows him in 28:81.

The section says ascent comes by using wealth to turn toward the lowly; 28:77 tells Qarun to seek the Hereafter with what God gave him and to do good, giving an explicit ethical direction to abundance.

After Qarun and his house are swallowed by earth in 28:81, 28:82 says onlookers recognize that God expands and restricts provision. It reverses their envy of his wealth and echoes the section's shared plane of plenty and want.

The section's “مَالًا لُّبَدًا” makes gathered wealth a central image; 9:34 condemns hoarding gold and silver instead of spending in God's path, an explicit boundary between amassed property and beneficial use.
The section places rich and poor on the same earth; 9:35 turns hoarded gold and silver into a brand on the hoarders' bodies, reversing wealth from possession into punishment.
The section's poor person and its feeding deed belong to one scene; 2:215 answers what to spend by naming parents, kin, orphans, needy people, and travelers, specifying where property should flow.
The section presents helping the needy as the means of ascent; 30:38 commands giving relatives, the poor, and travelers their due, placing the share of the earthbound within the giver's property.

The section contrasts a person stuck to earth through plenty with one stuck through want; 59:9 praises people who give others preference even while themselves in need, reversing the expected direction of abundance.
The section makes the needy miskīn a recipient of the steep-pass act; 9:60 names the poor and needy among the recipients of alms, specifying a distribution of wealth toward those with little.

The section's road upward requires loosening one's grip on gathered wealth; 3:92 says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves, making the costly turn away from attachment explicit.

This is the setup for the section's cited 7:176: 7:175 introduces the person given God's signs who “فَانْسَلَخَ مِنْهَا”, so the next ayah's failure to rise by them reads as a chosen turning away from what could elevate him.
After the earth-clinging example in 7:176, 7:177 calls the example of those who deny God's signs evil; it completes the link the section draws between descent toward earth and denial of signs.

The section's lexicon says a bird can be l-b-d (ل ب د, B003), crouched on the earth; 67:19 instead shows birds above with wings spread and folded, a specific reversal from the section's grounded bird to flight.

The section links miskīn (س ك ن, B001) with stillness; 18:79 calls the boat owners “لِمَسَاكِينَ يَعْمَلُونَ فِي الْبَحْرِ”, poor people actively working at sea. Their movement marks a useful boundary: the Qur'anic poverty term does not itself mean motionless.

The section's lexicon calls l-b-d (ل ب د, B003) one who does not travel or leave; 4:100 describes emigrants finding broad room and provision in the earth, a direct movement away from being fixed in one place.

The section's BLD dictionary entry describes a camel kneeling with its chest on the ground; 88:17 opens a sequence by asking people to look at camels and how they were created, recalling the animal in the section's grounded image.
The section contrasts raised heights with words pressed to earth; 88:18 asks how the sky was raised, part of the same 88:17–20 sequence that moves from camel to heaven, mountains, and spread earth.
The section's image sets elevation against a low plane; 88:19 asks how mountains were erected within the sequence from camel to raised sky and spread earth, giving the high side of that contrast.
The section puts its images on the horizontal ground beneath the surah's elevations; 88:20 asks how the earth was spread, completing the neighboring camel/sky/mountain survey with the low plane.

The section's lexicon says rain packs the earth; 7:57 uses the word “لِبَلَدٍ مَيِّتٍ” for dead land that rain revives with fruit, a reversal in which rain makes ground productive rather than merely pressed down.

The section links البلد to ground and settlement; 7:58 uses “الْبَلَدُ الطَّيِّبُ” for good land that yields plants while bad land yields little, showing the ground's condition can make abundance or scarcity visible.
The section's piled wealth is set against the earth-bound poor; 18:45 pictures worldly life as rain-fed growth that dries and is scattered by wind, making abundant material life visibly temporary.

The section's root notes equate the dead person's turbah with the grave (ت ر ب, B001); 80:21 says God causes a person to die and be buried (“فَأَقْبَرَهُ”), directly naming what the soil-bound word leads to.
After 80:21's burial, 80:22 says God will raise the person when He wills; this neighboring ayah completes the section's contrast between being laid in earth and being elevated.
The section sets piled wealth alongside the poor who lack it; 4:37 condemns miserliness and concealing God's bounty, a specific reversal of property held close while others remain in need.

The section's moral turn is to give toward vulnerable people; 24:22 urges pardon and continued support for relatives, poor people, and migrants even after personal hurt, giving a concrete test of generosity.

The section pairs a claim of having spent heaps with care for the poor; 17:27 calls reckless spenders brothers of devils, marking a boundary between boastful depletion and directed aid such as 17:26 commands.
The section's wealth-rich man says he spent a great mass; 17:29 warns against a closed hand and against spending without limit, setting a boundary around the handling of wealth beside the poor's due.

The section juxtaposes abundant wealth with the needy person's lack; 25:67 describes good spending as neither wasteful nor miserly, a specific boundary that corrects both unbounded depletion and withholding.
The section says the steep pass opens through deeds for the lowly; 92:5 begins the contrast with one who gives and is God-fearing, tying expenditure to a moral route.
In the same sequence as the giver in 92:5, 92:6 says he affirms the best; this supplies the belief behind the section's contrast between mere wealth spent and giving that leads upward.
The section presents the steep pass as the hard route toward elevation; 92:7 says the giving person will be eased toward ease, an explicit reversal of the burdened earthward posture.
The section's rich figure is stuck in an abundance that does not raise him; 92:8 describes the opposite of the giver, one who is stingy and sees himself as self-sufficient.
In 92:8–10, the self-sufficient miser's stance is paired with denial of the good; 92:9 names that denial, clarifying the inner turn opposite to the section's ascent by compassion.
The section opposes ascent to being fixed toward the earth; 92:10 says the miser is eased toward hardship, an explicit path-reversal from 92:7's ease for the giver.
The section measures the rich man's mass of wealth against the poor person's soil; 92:11 says his wealth will not avail him when he falls, removing wealth's claim to rescue him.

The section's dictionary sense for لبد (ل ب د, B003) is one who does not travel or leave; 4:97 challenges people who remain behind by asking whether God's earth was spacious enough for them to migrate. The verse makes staying fixed a question of choice, unlike poverty that restricts movement.

The section's stillness image can describe being unable to move; 4:98 exempts men, women, and children who truly lack means and a way out. It marks the boundary between chosen attachment to the earth and constrained immobility.

The section explains لبد (ل ب د, B001) through felt made as fibers pressed into a layer and also names the person who stays put; 16:80 names wool and animal hair made into furnishings and homes as “سَكَنًا”. The verse supplies the material and dwelling side of that image, though it does not describe the felting process.

The section sets claimed wealth beside the poor person's need and makes giving a route upward; 63:10 urges spending from God's provision before death arrives, when the regretful person wishes for more time to give charity.

The section's man says he spent a mass of wealth, while the needy require compassionate help; 2:262 says spending should not be followed by reminders or injury. In the neighboring charity passage, it distinguishes aid from a self-promoting claim.

The section's ascent depends on turning toward the earthbound poor with mercy; 2:263 says a kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, defining the manner of aid in the charitable sequence that continues into 2:264.

The section links giving toward the needy with elevation; 2:274 describes spending wealth by night and day, privately and publicly, with reward from God. It continues the same charitable subject as 2:271, adding the steadiness of giving across circumstances.

The section's steep-pass deeds include freeing a neck from bondage; 3:180 says what misers withhold will be put around their necks. It reverses withheld wealth into constriction, opposite the section's act of release.

The section names freeing a captive as part of the passage upward; 24:33 tells owners to help enslaved people seeking emancipation from the property God has given them, making wealth a means of release.

The section treats riches and poverty as a shared earthly condition and makes turning wealth outward a source of ascent; 47:38 says people called to spend who withhold only withhold from themselves, since God is rich and they are needy.

The section contrasts a mass of wealth kept at ground level with the deed that raises a person; 2:261 depicts spending for God as seed bearing seven ears with many grains, turning the spent possession into multiplied yield.

The section opposes piled wealth to giving that carries a person upward; 64:16 urges spending from God's provision and says those protected from their own greed are successful, naming the inward obstacle to releasing wealth.

The section's steep-pass sequence feeds a person in need on a day of hunger; 2:184 makes feeding a poor person an alternative obligation for those who cannot fast, another specific way food reaches the miskīn.
The section makes feeding the needy part of its moral ascent; 5:89 requires feeding ten poor people as one expiation for a broken oath, giving a concrete instance of wealth converted into food.

The section's imagery includes a camel kneeling and feeding the poor; 5:95 includes feeding poor people as an expiation for a hunting violation during pilgrimage, linking a costly animal-related act to provision for those in need.

The section names feeding the hungry and the poor as the steep-pass work; 22:28 tells pilgrims to eat from sacrificial livestock and feed the needy who ask, an earlier formulation in the same sacrificial passage as 22:36.

The section sets amassed wealth beside people in need; 4:8 says that when inheritance is being divided and relatives, orphans, and poor people are present, they should be given something from it, directing property toward those with little.
The section's lexicon says a bird can be لبد (ل ب د, B003), crouched on the ground; 16:79 instead points to birds held in the sky, a specific reversal from the grounded bird to one borne aloft.

The section places a rich man and a poor person on the same earthly plane; 16:71 asks why people given more provision do not share it with those under their authority, presenting unequal provision as a relationship of withheld goods.

The section distinguishes earthly wealth from the ascent made through mercy and help; 43:32 says God apportions provision and raises some people above others in worldly ranks, yet God's mercy is better than what they accumulate.

The section's settled-place and wealth imagery meets people made poor by displacement; 59:8 describes needy emigrants driven from their homes and property who seek God's bounty. It supplies the migrants' own loss that 59:9's generosity answers.
The section's wealthy man boasts of having spent “مَالًا لُّبَدًا”; 18:34 gives the garden owner’s comparison, “أَنَا أَكْثَرُ مِنكَ مَالًا”, making wealth a basis for status over another person.

The section places abundant wealth beside the poor person's earth-bound state; 18:35 has the garden owner enter his property convinced it will never perish, exposing the false permanence that the section's grave and soil senses unsettle.

The section's dictionary also gives the reversal “no little or much” for לبد (ل ب د, B007); 18:42 depicts the garden owner's fruit and wealth destroyed, leaving him regretful over what he had spent. The former abundance collapses toward nothing.
